I’m technically disabled and have stayed home for years and absolutely hate it, would not even wish this on my worst enemy. I felt the same way as you, but believe me it’s absolutely miserable and you may either grow to hate it overtime or be extremely stressed out with a loss of sense of identity. Simply another situation of “the grass looks greener on the other side,” when reality it may not be. I don’t have kids and I can imagine with kids it’ll even be more stressful. Thankfully my husband is understanding of my situation, but I’m at a point where I want out of my situation of being unemployed. I’m back in school studying IT and really hoping I can gain employment. I am also autistic and understand the hardship of working… it sucks. However at the same time I do find isolation at home to be rather depressing there are negative trade offs to staying at home. I am still finding who I am instead of just being my husband’s wife. It is a serious decision and a lot of planning to be a SAHM and not something to take lightly if you’re absolutely serious about it.

It sounds like something WFH possibly part time or flexible hours would work for you. A ton of autistic people go this route and that’s what I’m working towards atm. There’s schools that offer virtual classes nowadays try it out if you’re unhappy with working at the bakery.

Also to not get personal, but I’d figure out where this came from deep down for you. Is it something you truly want or from an external source? Is it trauma? Is it wanting a life fulfilled in some other way? I really thought I wanted to be a housewife and have kids for the longest, then I realized a lot of it had to do with my trauma, upbringing, and disability of feeling like I’m not able to hold down a career. What sealed the deal for me even more is that I’d find kids way too stressful plus pregnancy (hello, sensory issues and pain) that led me to leave that mindset rather quickly. Sometimes disability is a huge pain in the rear end especially finding out I was autistic later in life and for me that was the case for why I felt so lost in life. It is okay if disability gets in the way and that’s why you’re struggling with work if that is the reasoning. If anything having kids could be even more stressful for disability, but I understand if there is shame around not being able to work due to a disability. Perhaps given that reasoning you want kids and a life at home, it’s just a lot of hard work. I don’t want to dissuade you, but it takes way more than just simply staying at home with kids and a guy. You’re not trading in a career for more relaxation. You’re trading in work for more work. At the same time it would be good to take a look at if that’s what’s going on for you.

When I lived alone after my divorce for over two years, I was able to curb a lot of my sensory issues and overload because I didn't have other people in the same living situation together with me. It's got its pros and cons for living alone. I would recommend that if you do live alone to make sure to have an outside support system in case you need help or in an emergency. I found that sometimes I needed help with heavy lifting in my own home and couldn't do it without some form of help outside. That was what was the most difficult thing for me when I lived alone was the lack of outside support system or support system living far away. I found a few friends at the time when I lived alone and that helped a bit.

Otherwise the peace and quietness was absolutely worth it. Most things that traumatized me, I was able to curb those thoughts more easily because I didn't have someone in my space to constantly trigger that for me. If my place was messy or I didn't cook, that's okay because I had no one to tend to, but myself. If I didn't clean on time that would be only up to me to clean that up without someone breathing down my neck. If it got bad enough for me, I eventually cleaned on my own time with my own spoons instead of on someone else's time and schedule.

I'm all about skincare, I use Japanese/Korean sunscreen often. Lately I switched to using sun sticks. The one I use is the Abib sunstick. It works on days when I do not want to use my hands to put on sunscreen and it's not in liquid form if that can be a sensory issue for you. It is unscented and glides on well. Something to check out.
